title: The 13 Most Haunted Places in New Orleans
excerpt: 13 most haunted places in New Orleans including the most haunted hotels, bars, and restaurants.
content:
Phantoms are lurking down in the bayou.

By

Carson Oliver | Published Nov 23, 2026

New Orleans is well-known for Mardi Gras, jazz music, and Cajun food, but it’s also regarded as perhaps the most haunted city in America. 

The city has a rich but convoluted cultural history, blending French and Spanish culture with African, Caribbean, and Creole influences. Walking through the old streets of New Orleans, there is a certain energy that you can find nowhere else.

Here are the 13 most haunted spots in The Big Easy, ranging from antique hotels to cemeteries and even bars.

When a fire broke out in 1834 at LaLaurie Mansion, the cause was unknown at first. The heartbreaking truth is that the fire was set by a 70-year-old enslaved cook who set the fire to free herself and her fellow slaves from their collective misery.

Delphine LaLaurie, the owner of the mansion, was unbelievably cruel. Witnesses discovered a private torture chamber where she would do unspeakable things to the people she enslaved. Unfortunately, LaLaurie fled after the fire and was not captured. 

But evil remained. Visitors have reported hearing screams and scratches from upstairs rooms. 

The mansion was also, at one time, the home of Nicolas Cage.

New Orleans is synonymous with voodoo culture in America. Originated from enslaved peoples, New Orleans derived its own brand of voodoo culture via mixing West African spiritual traditions with elements of Haitian practice and Catholicism. Perhaps no figure was more instrumental in voodoo’s newfound popularity than Laveau. 

The original property burned down, but you can still see the exterior of the rebuilt property. Residents have given accounts of feeling significant pressure on various parts of their body, almost as if someone was poking at them.

Modern day voodoo practitioners consider the house a sacred space.

If you’re looking for a bite to eat, Muriel’s can feed you and give you your fix of paranormal activity. The restaurant was the former home of Pierre Jourdan, who lost the house in a particularly unlucky hand of poker. 

Muriel’s has a dedicated séance room for those who want a direct line of communication with Mr. Jourdan. The restaurant also lays claim to a mischievous ghost at their bar, where patrons have seen glasses fly off the shelves.

The folks at Muriel's tend to view ghosts not as hellish presences but rather, as those who want to keep celebrating life and who love New Orleans too much to leave.

Back when my grandmother lived in New Orleans, she attended Ursuline high school, where the legend of the famous convent and the “Casket Girls” loomed large.

The Casket Girls come over with the first Ursuline nuns back in the early 1700s. Most strangely, the girls carried their possessions around in casket-shaped chests, but after the girls left the convent, legend has it that the caskets were empty. Many believe the caskets harbored vampires. 

The Catholic Church vehemently denies these rumors.

Right across from the Old Ursuline Convent, this house was the home of Confederate general P.G.T. Beauregard and prolific author Francis Parkinson Keyes, who finished over 30 novels while living there. It was also built for Joseph LeCarpentier, the grandfather of world-famous chess grandmaster Paul Morphy. 

Happenings here range from skirmishes between spectral soldiers, a lady in a white dress, and the smell of blood. This spot is a mainstay for ghost tour guides in New Orleans.

I’ve actually stayed in the Columns Hotel for a night, and while I didn’t directly encounter any presences, I can see how the hotel earned its reputation. It’s a lovely hotel, landing on the Michelin Guide in 2024 and 2025, but it certainly has a ghostly feel.

Hotel guests have reported a variety of sightings including dapper gentlemen, a little girl, and a woman in a white gown. It’s a must-visit for any ghost fanatic, and if you’d like, you can even rent a haunted room. 

The most notorious options include Room 21 and Room 10.

This cemetery is the final resting place for many famous New Orleanians including Homer Plessy and Marie Leveau. Because of the frequent flooding in the area, all the tombs are above-ground, making the cemetery different than your typical burial ground. 

You can easily get lost wandering between massive mausoleums and breathtaking statues. The cemetery offers its own in-house tours, including daytime and after-dark offerings.

Also, for those with some time to spare, St. Louis Cathedral across the street is supposedly frequented by phantom priests.

Lafitte’s claims it’s the oldest bar not just in New Orleans but in the entire country. It is one of the only structures to survive the great fires of New Orleans in 1788 and 1794 thanks to its slate roof. 

The bar was also a mainstay for privateer Jean Lafitte and his brother Pierre. And of course, with that extensive of a history, the denizens of the bar have witnessed many unexplainable happenings including phantasmagoric sailors and glowing eyes peering in from grates. 

The bar even lays claim to Lafitte appearing as a fully bodied apparition, considered a great rarity amongst fans of the paranormal.

Antoine’s is one of the most famous restaurants in all of New Orleans, known for inventing the now-beloved Oysters Rockefeller. Even Franklin Roosevelt and Pope John Paul II have popped in for some classic creole food. But clearly, founder Antoine Alciatore still isn’t satisfied. 

Alciatore’s ghost famously watches over the kitchen, making sure the kitchen staff maintains the restaurant’s original standard. And that Antoine’s is still competing with its rival restaurant Arnaud’s. 

Speaking of Arnaud’s…

Arnaud’s is the largest restaurant in all of New Orleans but despite its size, it still maintains exceptional quality. Count Arnaud Cazenave makes sure that stays the case, all while donning his trademark tuxedo. The Count is known for friendly pranks on guests, and for keeping an eye on Arnaud’s and Antoine’s.

And apparently, the business runs in the family. Guests have also seen the Count's daughter, Germaine, float around the tables as a misty figure.

“The Sultan” was Sultan Jean Baptiste LePrete. Upon purchasing his palace, LePrete through a party complete with lavish delights, plenty of guests, and corpses. Several partygoers were found dead including LePrete and his brother. 

The Sultan's brother's hand was said to be reaching up from the ground, clawing at the air as if begging for one last breath. To make things even stranger, no one ever discovered the culprit for these brutal murders.  

This is a privately owned property, but owners have testified to seeing dark figures and chilling presences lurking in the shadows.

This property has a long and jumbled history. The original building was turned to ash in the Great Friday Fire of the 1788. Then, it was Aleix’s Coffee House, a speakeasy. Finally, it was renamed to the “The Absinthe Room.” 

It’s hosted literary superstars such as Walt Whitman, Oscar Wilde, and Mark Twain. However, it has also hosted spectral icons such as Benjamin Butler, Marie Leveau, and Jean Lafitte. The Old Absinthe House is truly the best of both worlds.

From strange surgical devices to potent potions, this museum harbors a comprehensive history of New Orleans apothecaries. Walking around the space, it becomes clear that before the advent of modern medicine, the cure was often deadlier than the disease. Lead syringes and serrated razors adorn the shelves.

The museum was formerly the home of Louis Joseph Dufilho Jr., the first person to ever be licensed for pharmaceutical practice in Louisiana. He is still seen wandering the halls, tidying the objects, and occasionally throwing books.
